entry.title: Running the Tokyo Marathon: What 42.195 km Taught Me About Persistence

link.title: Running the Tokyo Marathon: What 42.195 km Taught Me About Persistence

entry.content:
On a cold February morning in 2024, I stood at the starting line of the Tokyo Marathon with 38,000 other runners. I had trained for months, but nothing prepares you for the moment when the crowd surges forward and 42.195 kilometers stretches out ahead of you.

Why I Decided to Run

I’m not a natural athlete. I played football (soccer) in university — I was the captain of the student international team — but distance running was never my thing. The idea of running for 4+ hours seemed absurd.

But I needed a challenge that was entirely outside my academic and professional life. Something physical, measurable, and with a clear finish line. The Tokyo Marathon lottery gave me a spot, and that was that.

The Training

Training for a marathon is an exercise in consistency. No single run matters much; what matters is showing up every week, rain or shine, for months.

Phase Weekly Distance Key Sessions
Base (Weeks 1–8) 30–40 km Easy runs, building aerobic base
Build (Weeks 9–16) 40–55 km Long runs, tempo runs, intervals
Peak (Weeks 17–20) 55–65 km Longest runs (30+ km)
Taper (Weeks 21–24) 20–30 km Reduce volume, maintain intensity

The hardest part wasn’t the physical effort — it was the time management. Fitting 5 runs per week around a master’s program and a job at Apple required planning every day down to the hour.

Race Day

The first 20 km felt easy. The crowd support in Tokyo is incredible — people line the entire route, handing out food, shouting encouragement, playing music.

At 30 km, I hit the wall. My legs felt like lead. Every step was a negotiation with myself: just keep moving. This is where marathon running becomes mental, not physical.

The last 5 km were the longest of my life. But crossing the finish line — that moment is indescribable. Not because of the medal, but because I proved to myself that I can commit to something for months and see it through.

What It Taught Me

  1. Consistency beats intensity — One great run doesn’t matter; 100 good runs do. The same is true for research and skill-building.
  2. The wall is real, and it’s mental — At 30 km, my body wanted to stop. My mind kept it going. In research, the “wall” is when experiments fail or results are ambiguous. Pushing through is the skill.
  3. Preparation is everything — Race day was the easy part. The 4 months of training were the real marathon. In academia, the paper is the race; the months of data analysis are the training.
  4. Community matters — Running with others, sharing tips, encouraging each other — it made the process bearable. The same is true for research: find your community.

What’s Next

I’m already thinking about my next challenge. Maybe a sub-4-hour marathon. Maybe a triathlon. The specific goal matters less than having one.

If you’re considering running a marathon — or any big goal that seems impossible — my advice is simple: start small, be consistent, and trust the process. The finish line comes faster than you think.
entry.summary: In 2024 I ran the Tokyo Marathon. Here's what the experience taught me about goal-setting, persistence, and the power of incremental progress.

entry.title: Life Between Two Worlds: Engineering and Social Science

link.title: Life Between Two Worlds: Engineering and Social Science

entry.content:
People often ask me why I switched from Applied Chemistry to Policy Science. The honest answer is: I didn’t switch. I expanded.

The Engineer’s Mindset

Four years of engineering at Tokai University taught me to think in systems. Break a problem into components. Model each component. Understand the interactions. Optimize. This way of thinking is permanent — it shapes how I approach everything, from research questions to team management at Apple.

Engineering also taught me humility: your model is always wrong, but some models are useful. The question isn’t “is this perfect?” but “does this help me make a better decision than I would without it?”

The Social Scientist’s Toolkit

When I arrived at Sophia University as a research student in 2022, I felt like I’d landed on a different planet. Social scientists didn’t talk about optimization or efficiency — they talked about institutions, incentives, and human behavior. They were skeptical of models that claimed to predict human systems.

That skepticism was valuable. It taught me that data without context is just numbers. A regression coefficient tells you what happened, but understanding why requires institutional knowledge, historical context, and qualitative understanding.

The Intersection

At Waseda, I found the intersection: policy science that uses rigorous quantitative methods but remains grounded in real-world institutional understanding. This is where I can bring my engineering toolkit — modeling, optimization, systems thinking — to questions that actually matter to people’s lives.

Some examples of questions that live at this intersection:

  • How do energy policies affect economic outcomes in resource-dependent regions?
  • Can we predict the impact of educational interventions using large-scale administrative data?
  • What econometric methods best identify causal effects in observational policy data?

The Apple Japan Dimension

Working at Apple Japan adds a third dimension. In a corporate environment, the questions are more immediate: how do we improve team performance? How do we communicate across cultures? But the method is the same — identify the problem from data, build a process, measure the outcome.

The difference is speed. In academia, a paper takes months. At Apple, a process improvement can be implemented in days. Both have value: academia for depth, industry for iteration.

The Challenge

The hardest part of being interdisciplinary is that you never fully belong to either world. Engineers think you’ve gone soft. Social scientists think you’re too quantitative. But I’ve come to see this as a feature, not a bug. The most interesting problems don’t respect disciplinary boundaries.

Advice for Anyone Considering a Similar Path

  1. Don’t abandon your first field — your engineering training is an asset, not a sunk cost
  2. Learn the language of your new field — every discipline has its vocabulary and norms
  3. Find problems, not methods — let the question drive the methodology, not the other way around
  4. Embrace the discomfort — feeling like an outsider means you’re seeing things others miss

The intersection of engineering and social science is not a compromise. It’s a vantage point.
entry.summary: On the challenges and rewards of straddling engineering and social science — and why the intersection is where the most interesting problems live.

entry.title: Quantitative Methods for Policy Analysis: A Practical Overview

link.title: Quantitative Methods for Policy Analysis: A Practical Overview

entry.content:
Policy analysis without data is just opinion. In this post, I want to share the quantitative methods I rely on in my research at Waseda University, and explain why each one matters.

The Foundation: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)

Everything starts with OLS regression. It’s the workhorse of econometrics — simple, interpretable, and surprisingly powerful when used correctly.

import statsmodels.api as sm

X = sm.add_constant(data['policy_variable'])
model = sm.OLS(data['outcome'], X).fit()
print(model.summary())

The key insight: OLS gives you not just a coefficient, but a confidence interval and a p-value. You know not just the direction of the effect, but how certain you are about it.

Beyond OLS: Fixed Effects and Instrumental Variables

Real-world policy data is messy. Countries, prefectures, and individuals differ in ways that simple regression can’t capture. That’s where fixed effects come in.

* Stata: Panel regression with entity fixed effects
xtreg outcome policy_var controls, fe robust

Instrumental variables (IV) address the thornier problem of endogeneity — when your policy variable is correlated with the error term. Finding a good instrument is an art, but when you do, it unlocks causal inference from observational data.

Large-Scale Data: When Traditional Methods Hit Their Limits

When you have hundreds of variables and millions of observations, traditional econometric methods start to strain. This is where I combine econometrics with machine learning:

  • LASSO for variable selection when you have too many predictors
  • Random Forests for non-linear interactions that OLS can’t capture
  • Gradient Boosting for maximum predictive accuracy

The critical difference from pure ML: in policy analysis, interpretability matters as much as accuracy. A model that predicts well but can’t explain why is useless for policy.

The Workflow

My typical workflow looks like this:

  1. Clean and explore — pandas for data wrangling, matplotlib/seaborn for visualization
  2. Model — Start with OLS, add complexity only when needed
  3. Validate — Cross-validation, robustness checks, sensitivity analysis
  4. Interpret — Translate coefficients into policy-relevant language

Tools I Use Daily

Tool Purpose Why
Python (pandas, statsmodels, scikit-learn) Data wrangling, ML, visualization Ecosystem, flexibility
Stata Econometric models, panel data Built-in methods, reproducibility
Jupyter Exploratory analysis Interactive, visual
Git Version control Reproducible research

The combination of Python and Stata gives me both flexibility and rigor — Python for exploration and ML, Stata for formal econometric estimation.

What’s Next

In future posts, I’ll dive deeper into specific methods — difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity, and synthetic control — with worked examples. Stay tuned.
entry.summary: An overview of the quantitative toolkit I use for policy prediction — from regression to machine learning, with practical examples in Python and Stata.

entry.title: From Applied Chemistry to Policy Science — My Journey So Far

link.title: From Applied Chemistry to Policy Science — My Journey So Far

entry.content:
Welcome to my personal website. This is the first post on what I hope will become a record of my journey through research, engineering, and life in Tokyo.

The Beginning: Language and Chemistry

My path to where I am today wasn’t a straight line. It started in 2016 when I enrolled at Hallym Japanese Language Institute, determined to build a life and career in Japan. After a year of intensive language study, I moved into Tokai University’s Japanese Language Research Department, and from there into the Faculty of Engineering, Department of Applied Chemistry.

Those four years at Tokai University were formative. I built a solid foundation in engineering and energy systems — learning to think like an engineer, to break down complex problems into manageable components, and to approach challenges with a systems mindset. This foundation later led to my work on digital twin modeling of syngas-to-methanol conversion, for which I received the Best Presentation Award at the International Scientific-Practical Conference on Sustainable Development Goals in 2023.

The Pivot: From Engineering to Social Science

After graduating from Tokai in 2022, I took a step that surprised even myself: I enrolled as a research student at Sophia University’s Graduate School of Global Studies. This was my first real exposure to the social sciences, and it opened my eyes to how much of the world’s most pressing problems require not just technical solutions, but policy and economic understanding.

This led me to Waseda University, where I was accepted as a MEXT (Japanese Government Scholarship) research student in the Graduate School of International Communication. The MEXT scholarship was a turning point — it gave me the freedom and support to pursue research full-time.

Waseda: Where It All Comes Together

In April 2024, I enrolled in Waseda University’s Graduate School of Social Sciences, specializing in Policy Science. Here, I finally found the intersection I’d been looking for — a place where my engineering background meets econometric analysis meets real-world policy questions.

My current work focuses on mathematical modeling for policy prediction using large-scale data with Python and Stata. The goal: to use data not just to describe the world, but to forecast how policy decisions will shape it.

Parallel Track: Apple Japan

Alongside my academic work, I joined Apple Japan in June 2024 as a Technical Expert. In this role, I lead team performance analysis and mentoring in a multilingual, multicultural environment. It’s a completely different kind of challenge from academic research — but the core skill is the same: identify the problem from the data, and build a process that maximizes outcomes.

What’s Next

I’m currently working toward CFA Level I certification, which will add financial analysis to my toolkit. My goal is to bring together the “engineering, economics, and practice” triad at a higher level — using quantitative analysis and global leadership to solve complex business and policy challenges.

If any of this resonates with you, I’d love to connect. You can reach me at garahanov@fuji.waseda.jp, on Twitter, or on GitHub.

Thanks for stopping by.
entry.summary: How I went from studying applied chemistry in Korea to pursuing a master's in policy science at Waseda University — and what I've learned along the way.
